issue.title: ELK: re-centred edge label overlaps a parallel edge after terminal straightening
issue.body: ### Description Since 12.1.0 (#8344), a label on an edge whose terminal jog was straightened is re-projected onto the straightened route. Straightening moves the edge out of the lane ELK reserved for its label, so when another edge runs alongside, the re-centred label's background covers it. `elk.straightenEdges: false` avoids it: the edge keeps its jog and the label sits in the reserved lane. Narrow nodes make it likelier (e.g. `flowchart.minNodeWidth: 0`, which restores mermaid 11 sizing), since edges leave a small node closer together. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Render the code sample below. 2. The `changes` label is centred between the two Draft ↔ Review edges, about 19px apart, and its box covers the `Draft --> Review` edge. 3. Add `'elk': {'straightenEdges': false}` to the init: the label sits clear of the forward edge. ### Screenshots 12.1.0 default: the `changes` label covers the `Draft --> Review` edge. With `elk.straightenEdges: false`: the edges keep their jogs and the label sits clear. ### Code Sample ```text %%{init: {'layout': 'elk', 'htmlLabels': false, 'flowchart': {'minNodeWidth': 0}}}%% flowchart LR A[Draft] --> B{Review} B -->|approved| C[Published] B -->|changes| A ``` ### Setup - Mermaid version: 12.1.0 - Browser and Version: headless Chromium via puppeteer-core 25.12.0 ### Suggested Solutions - Skip straightening an edge whose label would then overlap another edge. - Or leave labelled edges unstraightened, so the label stays in the lane ELK reserved.

issue.title: ELK layout: spacing and feedback-edge routing cannot be configured, and edges back into a subgraph go around it
issue.body:
### Description

With `layout: elk`, the options that decide how large a diagram gets and how its edges are routed are fixed in the renderer.
None of them can be set from the diagram config.
On diagrams with subgraphs and labelled edges, this gives layouts with a lot of empty space and long detours.
There is no way to tune them.

This issue collects the fixed values and one routing defect that follows from them.
It overlaps with #7930 (`nodeSpacing` and `rankSpacing` are ignored) and #5177 (no way to pass ELK layout options).

### Fixed values

All references are to `packages/mermaid/src/rendering-util/layout-algorithms/elk/render.ts` on `develop` at 69778e6e9.

| What | Value | Line |
|---|---|---|
| Root `spacing.baseValue` | 40 | 926 |
| Root `spacing.nodeNode`, `edgeNode`, `edgeNodeBetweenLayers` | not set (commented out) | 938-941 |
| Subgraph `spacing.baseValue` | 24 | 205, 397 |
| Subgraph `spacing.nodeNode` | 50 | 219, 423 |
| Subgraph `elk.layered.spacing.edgeNodeBetweenLayers` | 30 | 418 |
| Subgraph `elk.spacing.edgeEdge` | 20 | 421 |
| Edge labels | `edgeLabels.inline: true`, `edgeLabels.placement: CENTER` on every label | 1132 |
| `elk.layered.feedbackEdges`, port constraints | not set | - |

The flowchart `nodeSpacing` and `rankSpacing` settings are not read by the ELK renderer, so they do not help either (#7930).

### Routing defect: an edge back into a subgraph goes around the outside

Steps to reproduce:

```
---
config:
  layout: elk
---
flowchart TB
  S --> A
  subgraph G
    A --> B
    C
  end
  B --> X
  X --> C
```

Expected: `X --> C` is a short edge, with `C` placed so that the edge approaches it from below or from the side.

Actual: `X` is placed below `G`, and `X --> C` leaves `X`, runs up the right-hand side of `G` and enters `C` from the top.

The cause is how the compound graph is laid out.
With `INCLUDE_CHILDREN`, the subgraph `G` is one node of the parent graph.
There, `G --> X` and `X --> G` form a cycle, although the nodes inside do not (`A --> B --> X --> C`).
ELK breaks the cycle by reversing one edge and routes it into the input side of `G`.

The config options only choose which edge takes the detour:

| Setting | Result |
|---|---|
| default, `preset: depthFirst`, `cycleBreakingStrategy: DEPTH_FIRST` or `GREEDY_MODEL_ORDER` | `X --> C` goes around `G` and enters `C` from the top |
| `preset: legacy`, `cycleBreakingStrategy: GREEDY` | `X` moves above `G`; `B --> X` goes around `G` instead |
| `preset: modelOrder`, `cycleBreakingStrategy: MODEL_ORDER` or `INTERACTIVE` | both `S --> A` and `X --> C` go over the top of `G` |

In a c4-beta diagram (#7843) with the same graph, writing the last edge as `C <-- X` (same meaning, laid out in the other direction) removes the cycle.
`C` is then placed above `X` and the edge rises straight into it; the total edge length drops from 1,217 to 616 px.

The same happens whenever a node outside a subgraph both receives from it and sends to it.
In C4 terms: a neighbouring container consumes one component's output and feeds another component of the same container.

### Suggested direction

- Read `nodeSpacing` and `rankSpacing`, or add `elk.nodeSpacing`, `elk.edgeSpacing` and `elk.edgeNodeSpacing` keys to the `elk` config section.
- Decide feedback edges on the graph with subgraphs collapsed, before handing it to ELK.
  Pass such an edge to ELK in the downstream direction and keep the arrowhead at the original target.
  This is what the `C <-- X` rewrite does by hand.

### Setup

- Mermaid: a local build based on `develop` at 69778e6e9 that also carries the c4-beta changes of #7843; the files under `rendering-util/layout-algorithms/elk/` are identical to `develop`
- Browser: Chromium (Playwright)

When connecting nodes inside a sub-graph, you will get trouble linking the individual nodes to nodes outside their sub-graph. But there is a workaround that perfectly solves the problem for me:

If it's not absolutely necessary to connect nodes inside the sub-graph, you can specify the orthogonal direction and be fine with it, because Mermaid will think that these nodes are on the same hierarchy level and place them "next to each other". What "next to" means depends on your direction.

**Example:**
In this example, I want 2 parents to ALWAYS be next to each other on a horizontal level. This means, I will specify Top-to-bottom direction as a "level" in top-to-bottom means a horizontal level:

```mermaid
flowchart TB

subgraph Grandparents1
    direction TB
    grandma1 & grandpa1
end

subgraph Grandparents2
    direction TB
    grandma2 & grandpa2
end

subgraph Parents
    direction LR
    mother & father
end

You

Grandparents2 --> Uncle
Grandparents1 --> father
Grandparents2 --> mother

Parents --> You

```

Hope this might help y'all :)

issue.title: Flowcharts with subgraphs have many more edge crossings than needed
issue.body:
Flowcharts with subgraphs get a lot more edge crossings in Pele than in Mermaid's own layouts. It shows most when nodes in several subgraphs all connect to one shared node, like steps that read from and write to one store. The edges leave each subgraph in an order that has nothing to do with where they go next, so they cross on the way.

A small example:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  subgraph A
    a1 --> a2 --> a3 --> a4 --> a5
  end
  subgraph B
    b1 --> b2 --> b3 --> b4 --> b5
  end
  subgraph C
    store[(Store)]
  end
  a1 & a2 & a3 & a4 & a5 --> store
  b1 & b2 & b3 & b4 & b5 --> store
```

Pele 1.6.0 draws this with 22 crossings (20 with `curve: step`). Mermaid's ELK layout draws it with none.

As far as I can tell, the cause is in `src/layout/compound.ts`. Each subgraph is laid out on its own, from the inside out, and the ports on its border are ordered only by what is inside it. The level above then has to connect ports whose order it cannot change.

To measure it, I wrote ten flowcharts shaped like real architecture and pipeline diagrams: pipelines with subgraphs, many-to-one fan-ins, edges between subgraphs, error branches, TD and LR, 20 to 80 nodes. I counted crossings from the rendered SVG geometry. Two edges that share a node are not counted as crossing within 24px of it, or where they merge into one straight run into it. For reference I ran the same files through Mermaid 12.2 with dagre and with ELK.

The edge style changes the count a little, so I counted two styles. Mermaid's ELK layout always draws orthogonal edges with rounded corners and ignores `flowchart.curve`. Pele draws the same kind of edges with `curve: step`, so that is the like-for-like comparison. Dagre was run with `curve: step` there too. The second set uses each renderer's default: curves for Pele and dagre, and the same orthogonal edges for ELK.

| graph | Pele 1.6.0, step | dagre, step | ELK | Pele 1.6.0, curves | dagre, curves |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| storage fan-in, TD, 6 subgraphs | 62 | 49 | 6 | 66 | 7 |
| ETL, LR | 16 | 2 | 7 | 16 | 3 |
| services, TD | 16 | 35 | 11 | 16 | 17 |
| CI/CD, LR | 25 | 19 | 9 | 26 | 15 |
| request errors, TD, no subgraphs | 0 | 6 | 0 | 0 | 5 |
| data platform, LR, chain of 6 subgraphs | 85 | 87 | 53 | 90 | 68 |
| nested subgraphs, LR | 10 | 14 | 8 | 10 | 11 |
| ML pipeline, TD | 15 | 21 | 6 | 15 | 18 |
| mixed directions | 8 | 12 | 8 | 8 | 11 |
| random DAG, 60 nodes, no subgraphs | 33 | 61 | 24 | 33 | 47 |
| total | 270 | 306 | 132 | 280 | 202 |

Without subgraphs Pele is already close to ELK. With subgraphs it falls behind.

### Examples

Three of the benchmark flowcharts, drawn by Pele 1.6.0 with `curve: step` next to Mermaid's ELK layout, so that both draw the same kind of edges. Click an image for full size.

Storage fan-in, TD: 62 crossings in Pele 1.6.0, 6 in ELK. Steps in two subgraphs all read from and write to one store, and the edges cross on their way out of the subgraphs.

![Storage fan-in, Pele 1.6.0 with curve step, 62 crossings, and Mermaid ELK, 6 crossings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Spenhouet/pele/c546219c2bbadb9921a06f55e7b96ce8b7a41188/layout-crossings/issue-01-storage-fanin.png)

CI/CD, LR: 25 crossings in Pele 1.6.0, 9 in ELK.

![CI/CD pipeline, Pele 1.6.0 with curve step, 25 crossings, and Mermaid ELK, 9 crossings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Spenhouet/pele/c546219c2bbadb9921a06f55e7b96ce8b7a41188/layout-crossings/issue-04-cicd-lr.png)

Data platform, LR, a chain of six subgraphs: 85 crossings in Pele 1.6.0, 53 in ELK.

![Data platform, Pele 1.6.0 with curve step, 85 crossings, and Mermaid ELK, 53 crossings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Spenhouet/pele/c546219c2bbadb9921a06f55e7b96ce8b7a41188/layout-crossings/issue-06-data-platform.png)

I have a change that brings the totals down to 141 with `curve: step` and 147 with curves. It opens no new crossings in the drawings from Mermaid's docs or in the playground cases. The PR is #4. It costs layout time on drawings with subgraphs, so that trade-off is yours to judge. The benchmark files and the script that counts crossings are small, and I can add them to the repo if that is useful.

issue.title: Layout: fewer edge crossings in drawings with subgraphs
issue.body:
Closes #3.

Three commits.

**Layout: Swap neighbouring nodes where that crosses less.** After the barycenter sweeps, small graphs (the ones that already get the second sweep run) get a pass that swaps two neighbours in a rank when they cross less the other way round. The new order is kept only if the total count drops. On its own this does not change the ten benchmark graphs from the issue. It gives about 1% fewer crossings on random graphs. None of the drawings from Mermaid's docs or the playground cases change.

**Layout: Order groups and their border ports from a layout of the whole drawing.** This is the main change, all in `compound.ts` plus a few hooks in `layered.ts`:

1. Before the groups are laid out, the whole drawing is ordered once as one flat graph (`layered` with the new `groups` and `orderOnly` options). The nodes of each group stay side by side in every rank while the crossings are reduced. Each node then has a place across the flow, and a group's place is the average of its nodes'.
2. Each level starts from that order (`LNode.key`). The ports on the far side of a group, for edges that leave it, are held in the order in which those edges leave the group in the flat layout (`LNode.hint`, and a rank of ports that all have one keeps that order).
3. If the result crosses much more than the flat layout did, the drawing is also laid out the old way, and the one that crosses less is kept.
4. Where a group sends more than one edge out through its far side, the drawing is laid out once more with those ports in the order of where their edges went, and kept if it crosses less. This is what fixes fans from several groups into one node.

**Layout: Order ports by where a stepped edge turns, not by its first point.** With `curve: step`, the point after a port is straight below it on the edge's track, so step 4 kept the order it had. It now looks at the first point that is not in line with the port.

Crossings are counted on the routes (`routeCrossings`), with each curve taken as a few straight pieces. Two edges that share a node are not counted as crossing where they fan out from it. Step 1 only runs when every group runs the way the whole drawing does. All of this only runs for drawings with groups whose edges cross their borders, up to 500 edges and 400 ports. Without subgraphs nothing changes apart from the first commit.

Most of the `compound.ts` diff is indentation, because the old layout passes moved into a `place()` function that can run more than once. Viewing it with whitespace hidden makes it much shorter.

### Crossings

Counted from the rendered SVG geometry, the same way as in the issue. Mermaid's ELK layout always draws orthogonal edges with rounded corners, so the like-for-like comparison is Pele with `curve: step`, which draws the same kind of edges. Dagre was run with `curve: step` too.

| graph | before, step | after, step | dagre, step | ELK |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| storage fan-in, TD | 62 | 8 | 49 | 6 |
| ETL, LR | 16 | 12 | 2 | 7 |
| services, TD | 16 | 11 | 35 | 11 |
| CI/CD, LR | 25 | 9 | 19 | 9 |
| request errors, TD | 0 | 0 | 6 | 0 |
| data platform, LR | 85 | 40 | 87 | 53 |
| nested subgraphs, LR | 10 | 10 | 14 | 8 |
| ML pipeline, TD | 15 | 10 | 21 | 6 |
| mixed directions | 8 | 8 | 12 | 8 |
| random DAG, 60 nodes | 33 | 33 | 61 | 24 |
| total | 270 | 141 | 306 | 132 |

With the default curves (dagre with its default curves as well):

| graph | before | after | dagre |
|---|---|---|---|
| storage fan-in, TD | 66 | 10 | 7 |
| ETL, LR | 16 | 7 | 3 |
| services, TD | 16 | 14 | 17 |
| CI/CD, LR | 26 | 11 | 15 |
| request errors, TD | 0 | 0 | 5 |
| data platform, LR | 90 | 41 | 68 |
| nested subgraphs, LR | 10 | 10 | 11 |
| ML pipeline, TD | 15 | 13 | 18 |
| mixed directions | 8 | 8 | 11 |
| random DAG, 60 nodes | 33 | 33 | 47 |
| total | 280 | 147 | 202 |

The example from the issue goes from 20 crossings to 0 with `curve: step`, and from 22 to 4 with curves. On 24 random flowcharts with subgraphs (20 to 60 nodes, groups picked at random, so harder than real diagrams) the total goes from 4884 to 4430 with `curve: step` and from 5039 to 4531 with curves. One graph gets 2 more crossings in each style. Edge length and bends stay about the same.

In Mermaid's docs examples and the playground layout cases (flowchart, state, class, ER, requirement, use case and agentflow, 312 drawings) no drawing crosses more than before. Four of them are drawn differently: flowchart docs examples 6, 7 and 98, and use case example 22. Example 98 loses its wiggles. In 6 and 7 the client group puts its two nodes side by side instead of one above the other.

### Time

This is the cost. Drawings with groups whose edges cross their borders are laid out two or three times instead of once.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the ten benchmark flowcharts, median per render, curves | 21.9 ms total | 44.0 ms total |
| the same with `curve: step` | 20.7 ms total | 40.1 ms total |

issue.body:
### Problem statement

I'm writing a small VST plugin for taking project notes using markdown. Being able to include things like flow diagrams for filter chains is super userful so I figured I'd add merman for that, only to discover it tacks almost 5MB onto the binary, which makes... very little sense if all I need is one or two diagram types =)

### Proposed change

It would be very useful to make it so that every diagram can be included/excluded via a config: it's great that it's all there, but it would be even better if there was a way to drop anything that isn't necessary for the specific use case.

### Impact on parity / performance

No parity or performance impact as such, other than builds yielding much smaller binaries, which is probably a worthwhile goal?

### Alternatives considered

I ended up just forking and making Fable 5.1 strip the code down to what my project needed, which is just flowcharts and gannt. Removing the 28ish unused diagram types dropped my final binary by 4.74MB, 

### Additional context

While "generic editors" need to support all mermaid charts, not everything that needs to show or even edit markdown is a full editor, and many contexts don't need more than one or two very domain-specific chart types.

In my case, music project documentation mostly needs to be able to show delivery timelines and instrument/filter chains, and not much else, so a few hundred KB is all that needs to meet the mermaid-in-markdown requirements.

Thanks for reporting this!

PR #149 adds compile-time diagram-family selection through Cargo features. You can now include only the Mermaid families your application needs, while keeping output and layout features separate.

For a Flowchart + Gantt SVG application:

```toml
[dependencies]
merman = {
    version = "0.8.0-alpha.7",
    default-features = false,
    features = [
        "svg",
        "diagram-flowchart",
        "diagram-gantt",
    ],
}
````

This enables the Flowchart and Gantt implementations without enabling the other diagram families. If you only need parsing, you can depend on `merman-core` directly:

```toml
[dependencies]
merman-core = {
    version = "0.8.0-alpha.7",
    default-features = false,
    features = ["diagram-gantt"],
}
```

Applications using the normal `merman` defaults do not need to change anything. The default configuration continues to include all diagram families.

I also measured the resulting native executable using the same runtime-fed consumer, Rust 1.95.0, the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` target, and the same release settings:

- All diagrams + SVG: 9,725,440 bytes
- Flowchart + Gantt + SVG: 5,411,328 bytes
- Reduction: 4,314,112 bytes, or 44.359%

The selected Flowchart and Gantt SVG outputs matched the full build, and Sequence input was rejected as an unsupported diagram in the reduced build.

The feature is planned for `v0.8.0-alpha.7`. I think this is the right way to solve the problem. :)

issue.title: feat(svg): lightweight built-in layout so SVG flowcharts work without elkjs
issue.body:
## Problem

SVG output for flowchart, state, class, ER and architecture diagrams requires `elkjs` (about 1.5 MB minified). Without it, `renderMermaidSVG` throws `ElkNotRegisteredError` (see `packages/svg-renderer/src/__tests__/elk-optional-peer-1370.test.ts`). Users who only want SVG flowcharts in a size-sensitive bundle have no lighter option. ASCII output and the non-graph SVG types (sequence, pie, xychart, C4) already work without `elkjs`.

## Idea

Add a small built-in layered layout (dagre-style: rank assignment, crossing reduction, coordinate assignment) as an alternative engine for at least flowcharts, so SVG works without registering `elkjs`.

## Open questions

- Which diagram types to cover first (flowchart only, or state too, since it shares the graph model)?
- Opt-in (`layout: 'simple'`) or automatic fallback when `elkjs` is not registered?
- Acceptable layout-quality gap versus ELK, and how it shows up in SVG snapshots (every case needs SVG and ASCII snapshots).
- Target size budget, measured against the Bundle Size section of the README.

## Context

Raised in review of #1646 (https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/pull/1646#discussion_r4238757777): "Could we provide an option that doesn't require elk and results in a much smaller dependency size?" The docs side was handled in that PR (f97b9346); this issue tracks the code option.

comments.body: might be a duplicate of #6024

After taking a look at the above issue and the one outlined in #6024, the underlying causes are different and should be considered separately. 

The problem in this scenario is that the parser should technically be throwing an error, despite it looking valid. 

One of the limitations of the underlying engine used for generating the layouts is that to enforce a clean grid pattern, each node needs to be no more then one "unit" away in X and Y direction. 

To make it a bit more clear, I changed the 3rd edge from `lambda1:R -[3]-> L:dynamodb` to `lambda1:R -[3]-> T:dynamodb`

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/81cf4e7a-9a62-4f40-bf63-5f54ddb844a6)

In this case, we'll call `client` the origin at `[0, 0]`. That means `api` is at `[1, 0]`, `lambda1` at `[2, 0]`, and `dynamodb` is at `[3, 1]`.

The issue lies in that `s3` is located at `[1, 2]`, where the y difference of the connecting node (`server` at `[0, 0]`) is greater then 1. This causes the constraints keeping the consistent grid pattern to fall apart and cause the unpredictable rendering we see.

Without using junctions, another way to fix this would be to replace edge 6 with `lambda2:R -[6]-> L:dynamodb` and keep the above change:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/23a5750a-e7d1-40eb-b018-2a8302d7a053)

Which now moves `s3` to position `[1, 1]` behind the scenes.

Obviously this behavior isn't ideal. Once I have more time I'll re-evaluate the options for layout engines to see if there's anything better but that probably won't happen until early in the summer.

In the meantime, I plan to make 2 changes to rectify the above issue:
1. Make the docs a lot more clear about this limitation. I'll make a few visual aids to avoid having to bring up the underlying coordinate system.
2. Add a check to detect jumps greater then 1 and throw an error.

> One of the limitations of the underlying engine used for generating the layouts is that to enforce a clean grid pattern, each node needs to be no more then one "unit" away in X and Y direction.

This one is a massive limitation as of now, should be clearly stated in the documentation introduction

For AI-generated or code-generated architecture diagrams, this limitation probably needs to be surfaced before rendering, not only after a confusing visual result appears.

A practical authoring-side validation could be:

1. build the intended relationship graph first
2. infer the grid hops implied by each relationship
3. flag any edge where `abs(dx) > 1` or `abs(dy) > 1`
4. either reject with a clear diagnostic or insert an explicit junction node as a routing hint

That would be especially useful for generated AWS / cloud diagrams where a model often emits the semantic dependencies correctly but does not understand the layout engine's hidden grid constraints.

The diagnostic could be phrased in architecture terms instead of coordinate terms, for example:

- `lambda2 -> dynamodb crosses more than one grid step; add an explicit junction or route through an adjacent service`
- `s3 is being positioned too far from the origin for this direct relationship; split the path or adjust source/target ports`

This would make the limitation much easier for users and generators to recover from. It also gives test fixtures a cleaner pass/fail condition: generated diagrams should be deterministic, or fail with an actionable routing diagnostic instead of sometimes rendering differently on refresh.

issue.title: graph TD + curly braces in a label misdetects as DOT — all node labels silently dropped
issue.body:
Any diagram that uses the legacy graph TD/graph TB header (rather than flowchart) and contains curly braces inside a quoted node label gets silently rerouted to the DOT/Graphviz-interop parser instead of the mermaid flowchart parser. Minimal repro: graph TD A["captures {binding} tokens"] --> B["done"] fm-cli detect reports Diagram type: flowchart but Method: DOT format detected, and fm-cli render --format svg then emits a diagram whose nodes show only the bare IDs (A, B) — every bracket label is dropped. On a larger real-world diagram (~35 lines, subgraphs,
in labels), the DOT path also invents phantom nodes from tokens it can't parse (e.g. a node whose first line is :start (config + :seed) produced an extra node rendered as START_-.) and prints subgraph titles unparsed (GROUP["one group — …"] as literal title text). There is no warning or diagnostic at any point, and fm-cli validate passes the file, so the mangling is invisible until you look at the output. Removing either trigger fixes it: changing the header to flowchart TD yields Method: explicit keyword match and a faithful render (verified side-by-side against mermaid.js 11), as does removing the {…} from the label. Presumably the DOT-detection heuristic sees the braces, and the ambiguous graph keyword (shared with DOT) lets the reclassification win over the mermaid header. Environment: v0.2.0 built from main @ d369a3f3 with cargo +nightly install --git --locked frankenmermaid-cli (rustc 1.100.0-nightly, 2026-08-24), macOS arm64 (aarch64-apple-darwin); defaults everywhere — no config file, no --parse-mode or layout flags.

comments.body: Fixed in 09196bef. The DOT probe classified any input as DOT when its first line began with graph/digraph/strict and braces appeared anywhere in the text, so the legacy `graph TD` header plus `{...}` inside a quoted label was rerouted to the DOT parser and every bracket label was dropped. Detection now follows the DOT header grammar: input is DOT only when the body-opening `{` sits where the grammar puts it — after the optional graph name (identifier, quoted, concatenated-quoted, or HTML name) — and the text ends with the body's closing `}`. Your repro now detects as `Method: explicit keyword match` and renders both labels; a real DOT graph that happens to be named TD/LR still detects as DOT. Regression tests cover the repro, direction-like DOT names, header fragments, and unterminated names. Please build from main; reopen if anything still misdetects.

issue.title: Class diagram (ELK layout): cardinality label overlaps the neighbouring edge when relations leave adjacent ports
issue.body: ### Description Follow-up to #8334 (fix for #8329). With the ELK layout, when two relations leave the same class from adjacent ports, ELK can place one relation's cardinality (end label) across the neighbouring edge's line. That makes the label hard to read. In the example below, Customer's `0..1` (on the `lives at` relation) is placed to the right of its port, and the `places` edge, which leaves the next port about 44px over, runs straight through it. ELK's layered end-label placement (`edgeLabels.placement: TAIL/HEAD`, used since #8334) reserves room beside the port but doesn't avoid other edges. I tried `elk.spacing.portPort` on the node, `elk.portLabels.placement`, `elk.spacing.edgeLabel` and `elk.layered.edgeLabels.sideSelection`, and none of them changed the placement. This is not a regression: before #8334 these labels were drawn under the class boxes. ### Steps to reproduce ```mermaid --- config: layout: elk --- classDiagram namespace Shop { class Customer class Order } namespace Catalog { class Product } Customer "1" --> "*" Order : places Order "*" --> "1..*" Product : contains Customer "0..1" -- "1" Address : lives at ``` This diagram is the `ELK-6` e2e case in `e2e/rendering/class/classDiagram-elk-v3.spec.js`. ### Expected behavior End labels of relations that leave neighbouring ports don't overlap each other's edge lines. For example, ports could be spaced to fit the labels, or a label could flip to the free side of its edge. ### Screenshots ### Mermaid version develop, with #8334 applied

First of all lets show the need for this solution. Normally, Mermaid nodes that are defined first are placed higher in the hierarchy. This can be overridden by Mermaid itself when there are subgraphs present, because for some reason subgraphs get higher levels in the hierarchy of nodes, even if they are defined after and should therefore come after in the hierarchy.

The basic black box process diagram shows a process as a "black box", in which the process receives inputs and produces outputs. Also, a "black box" process can feed itself by connecting its output to its input. The straightforward way to write a "black box" process diagram (that feeds itself) in Mermaid is:

``` mermaid
flowchart LR
  Input --> Process
  subgraph Process
    A --> B --> C --> A
  end
  Process --> Output
  Output --> Input
```
This produces the following image:
![o2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/52269801/115100967-27209900-9f06-11eb-9942-47f035556b2e.png)

As can be seen, the Input is not in to the left anymore, because its place in the hierarchy has been taken by the subgraph.

Giving credit to @XertroV the fixed Mermaid code is

``` mermaid
flowchart TB
  Input
  subgraph s1 [" "]
    Input --> Process
    subgraph s2 [" "]
      subgraph Process
        A --> B --> C --> A
      end
      Process --> Output
    end
  end
  Output --> Input
  
  classDef class1 fill: white, stroke: white
  class s1,s2 class1
  style Process fill: white, stroke: black
```

![o1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/52269801/115101004-72d34280-9f06-11eb-8674-014ab8af99f2.png)

issue.body:
Note: this is basically a clone of https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/issues/418 that was automatically closed as stale without resolution, even though there was an acknowledgement that this was an important function to have.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I need a way to specify that two or more nodes should be placed at the same level/rank 

For example, in the following graph I would like `b` and `c` to be on the same level

```
graph TD
a --> b & c
b --> d & c
c --> e & b
```

this currently yields something like the following graphs (notice how `b` and `c` are at different heights)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/408018/197999331-aef54dee-50d1-461b-89fd-d12b5e97af4e.png) 

**Describe the solution you'd like**

 I would like `b` and `c` to behave like in this diagram (notice how these two nodes are at the same height)

```
graph TD
a --> b & c
b --> d
c --> e
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/408018/197998812-05f07342-080d-4d7a-a00d-21dc43ecabde.png)

This is obviously an extremely simplified example. The real use cases have many more nodes, and being able to specify which ones should be at the same level is very important for the intelligibility of the output.

Any of these two solutions would work for me:

1. mermaid should recognize that there is no reason to put c on a lower rank than b (or vice-versa) and that therefore those two nodes should have the same rank (i.e. same height)
2. mermaid should support a way for the user to specify that two nodes should have the same rank, and place these nodes at the same level when rendering


**Describe alternatives you've considered**

graphviz allows to do this by specifying [`rank=same`](https://graphviz.org/docs/attrs/rank/)

I also tried with mermaid subgraphs but it does not yield a better outcome.

```
graph TD
subgraph x; b; c; end
a --> b & c
b --> d & c
c --> e & b
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/408018/198000484-645a22f2-e74e-4d37-8220-3b6c4cc615f5.png)


**Additional context**

The lack of this feature has forced me to use other tools for rendering category theory graphs.  One of the most fundamental structures in category theory is the commuting square.  This square is represented _exactly_ the same in every category theory reference I've ever come across:

    A   -- f -->  B
    |             |
    g             g'
    |             |
    v             v
    A'  -- f' --> B'

Hence the term commuting _square_.  Mermaid renders this as

```mermaid
%%{ init: {'flowchart': {'curve': 'linear' } } }%%
    graph LR;
      A -- f --> B
      A' -- f' --> B'
     A -- g --> A'
```

pr.title: Layout: fewer edge crossings in drawings with subgraphs
pr.body:
Closes #3.

Three commits.

**Layout: Swap neighbouring nodes where that crosses less.** After the barycenter sweeps, small graphs (the ones that already get the second sweep run) get a pass that swaps two neighbours in a rank when they cross less the other way round. The new order is kept only if the total count drops. On its own this does not change the ten benchmark graphs from the issue. It gives about 1% fewer crossings on random graphs. None of the drawings from Mermaid's docs or the playground cases change.

**Layout: Order groups and their border ports from a layout of the whole drawing.** This is the main change, all in `compound.ts` plus a few hooks in `layered.ts`:

1. Before the groups are laid out, the whole drawing is ordered once as one flat graph (`layered` with the new `groups` and `orderOnly` options). The nodes of each group stay side by side in every rank while the crossings are reduced. Each node then has a place across the flow, and a group's place is the average of its nodes'.
2. Each level starts from that order (`LNode.key`). The ports on the far side of a group, for edges that leave it, are held in the order in which those edges leave the group in the flat layout (`LNode.hint`, and a rank of ports that all have one keeps that order).
3. If the result crosses much more than the flat layout did, the drawing is also laid out the old way, and the one that crosses less is kept.
4. Where a group sends more than one edge out through its far side, the drawing is laid out once more with those ports in the order of where their edges went, and kept if it crosses less. This is what fixes fans from several groups into one node.

**Layout: Order ports by where a stepped edge turns, not by its first point.** With `curve: step`, the point after a port is straight below it on the edge's track, so step 4 kept the order it had. It now looks at the first point that is not in line with the port.

Crossings are counted on the routes (`routeCrossings`), with each curve taken as a few straight pieces. Two edges that share a node are not counted as crossing where they fan out from it. Step 1 only runs when every group runs the way the whole drawing does. All of this only runs for drawings with groups whose edges cross their borders, up to 500 edges and 400 ports. Without subgraphs nothing changes apart from the first commit.

Most of the `compound.ts` diff is indentation, because the old layout passes moved into a `place()` function that can run more than once. Viewing it with whitespace hidden makes it much shorter.

### Crossings

Counted from the rendered SVG geometry, the same way as in the issue. Mermaid's ELK layout always draws orthogonal edges with rounded corners, so the like-for-like comparison is Pele with `curve: step`, which draws the same kind of edges. Dagre was run with `curve: step` too.

| graph | before, step | after, step | dagre, step | ELK |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| storage fan-in, TD | 62 | 8 | 49 | 6 |
| ETL, LR | 16 | 12 | 2 | 7 |
| services, TD | 16 | 11 | 35 | 11 |
| CI/CD, LR | 25 | 9 | 19 | 9 |
| request errors, TD | 0 | 0 | 6 | 0 |
| data platform, LR | 85 | 40 | 87 | 53 |
| nested subgraphs, LR | 10 | 10 | 14 | 8 |
| ML pipeline, TD | 15 | 10 | 21 | 6 |
| mixed directions | 8 | 8 | 12 | 8 |
| random DAG, 60 nodes | 33 | 33 | 61 | 24 |
| total | 270 | 141 | 306 | 132 |

With the default curves (dagre with its default curves as well):

| graph | before | after | dagre |
|---|---|---|---|
| storage fan-in, TD | 66 | 10 | 7 |
| ETL, LR | 16 | 7 | 3 |
| services, TD | 16 | 14 | 17 |
| CI/CD, LR | 26 | 11 | 15 |
| request errors, TD | 0 | 0 | 5 |
| data platform, LR | 90 | 41 | 68 |
| nested subgraphs, LR | 10 | 10 | 11 |
| ML pipeline, TD | 15 | 13 | 18 |
| mixed directions | 8 | 8 | 11 |
| random DAG, 60 nodes | 33 | 33 | 47 |
| total | 280 | 147 | 202 |

The example from the issue goes from 20 crossings to 0 with `curve: step`, and from 22 to 4 with curves. On 24 random flowcharts with subgraphs (20 to 60 nodes, groups picked at random, so harder than real diagrams) the total goes from 4884 to 4430 with `curve: step` and from 5039 to 4531 with curves. One graph gets 2 more crossings in each style. Edge length and bends stay about the same.

In Mermaid's docs examples and the playground layout cases (flowchart, state, class, ER, requirement, use case and agentflow, 312 drawings) no drawing crosses more than before. Four of them are drawn differently: flowchart docs examples 6, 7 and 98, and use case example 22. Example 98 loses its wiggles. In 6 and 7 the client group puts its two nodes side by side instead of one above the other.

### Time

This is the cost. Drawings with groups whose edges cross their borders are laid out two or three times instead of once.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the ten benchmark flowcharts, median per render, curves | 21.9 ms total | 44.0 ms total |
| the same with `curve: step` | 20.7 ms total | 40.1 ms total |
| storage fan-in alone | 3.7 ms | 9.5 ms |
| `npm run bench` docs examples | 7.6 ms | 8.6 ms |
| mesh 500 nodes, tree 500 nodes | 27.8 ms, 9.5 ms | 27.6 ms, 9.7 ms |

Flat graphs are within noise. The stress tests pass in about the same time as before. The 400 ports and 500 edges limits keep large drawings to one layout. If the cost is too much, steps 3 and 4 are the expensive ones, and they could get a lower limit.

### Tests

I added tests in `tests/layout/compound.test.ts` for the crossing count, for a fan from two groups into a node in a third one (the order in which the edges leave their groups must match the order in which they enter the store's group, in TB and LR), and for a row of three groups whose nodes are written in an order that would cross. The fan test fails without this change. `npm test` and `npm run typecheck` pass. With the full suite running in parallel, `3,000 transitions into a ring of 1,200 composites` in `tests/state/stress.test.ts` sometimes goes over its 3 second limit on my machine, before and after this change. Run on its own, it takes about 0.5 s either way. I did not run `npm run test:website`.

pr.title: feat: add selectable diagram-family features
pr.body:
Closes #148

## What changed

Merman now supports compile-time selection of Mermaid diagram families through positive Cargo features. Each logical built-in family has a `diagram-*` selector, and `all-diagrams` is their canonical union.

The selectors are carried through the existing crate graph. Core and other low-level crates can compile no built-in families, one family, or a chosen subset. Family-exclusive parsers, semantic models, editor integrations, layout paths, and output handlers are conditionally compiled at their ownership boundaries.

Output and runtime capabilities remain separate feature axes:

- `svg`, `ascii`, `analysis`, `editor`, and binary export features select operations.
- `layout-cytoscape`, `layout-elk`, and `math` select rendering capabilities.
- Diagram selectors do not implicitly enable an output format, layout engine, math backend, or system adapter.

The default `merman`, CLI, and Rustdoc product recipes retain their complete-family behavior. `complete-svg` continues to describe SVG, Cytoscape, and math capabilities; it does not select diagram families.

The implementation keeps the family contract consistent across artifact profiles, Rustdoc, CLI, FFI, UniFFI, WASM, Web input manifests, Playground consumers, and CI validation. Cargo remains the feature resolver; no second feature solver was added.

## Compatibility and migration

Existing users with normal defaults do not need to change their manifests.

Users of low-level crates or `default-features = false` dependencies must explicitly select the parser families they need. Add `all-diagrams` to retain the previous complete parser surface, or select individual families:

```toml
[dependencies]
merman = { version = "...", default-features = false, features = ["svg", "diagram-flowchart", "diagram-gantt"] }
```

For parser-only use:

```toml
[dependencies]
merman-core = { version = "...", default-features = false, features = ["diagram-gantt"] }
```

Family-exclusive public model types and enum variants are now conditional on their owning selector. Consumers importing those types should enable the corresponding family and gate family-specific code as needed. `Error` and `CustomJson` infrastructure remains available without a built-in family.

Cargo features are additive across the dependency graph. A separate dependency edge that enables `all-diagrams` can widen the final application; `default-features = false` on one edge cannot remove features enabled elsewhere. Use `cargo tree -e features` and an isolated consumer when verifying an intended slim build.

This is a compile-time source and typed-API migration, not a runtime configuration switch. Published `0.8.0-alpha.6` packages predate these selectors; use the next release or a source checkout containing this change.

## Behavior and error contracts

- Strict parsing of a known disabled family returns `UnsupportedDiagram`.
- Suppressed parsing preserves the existing `Error` diagram behavior.
- Unknown input remains distinguishable from a known disabled family.
- A parser compiled in core does not imply that a local SVG or ASCII handler exists.
- Renderer and ASCII consumers return an explicit unsupported result when their local handler is absent.
- Cancellation, custom registry precedence, resource limits, and selected-family Mermaid behavior remain preserved.
- Shared implementation is retained where required. Flowchart and Swimlane share grammar/model code while retaining separate logical language admission.

## Validation

Local validation for commit `c183719c9` includes:

- Strict feature matrix: **619/619** build cases passed, covering no-family, all-family, every public family singleton, capability leaves, product recipes, and artifact profiles.
- Feature-matrix contract tests: **18/18** passed.
- Isolated renderer feature tests: **4/4** passed, including real `plan_render`, `prepare`, SVG output, disabled local handlers, and asymmetric core/renderer selection.
- Python performance contract suites: **212** tests passed.
- Native Windows release measurement using Rust 1.95.0 and the same runtime-fed consumer:
  - Candidate full (`all-diagrams,svg`): **9,725,440 bytes**.
  - Candidate Flowchart + Gantt (`diagram-flowchart,diagram-gantt,svg`): **5,411,328 bytes**.
  - The selected build is **4,314,112 bytes smaller (44.359%)** than the candidate full build.
  - Flowchart and Gantt input/SVG hashes match across the compared lanes; the subset reports `merman.parse.unsupported_diagram` for Sequence.
- The native measurement covers one Windows MSVC executable, release profile, target, and small corpus. It does not claim universal savings for WASM, mobile, VST, or other platforms.

Detailed migration guidance is in [`docs/FEATURES.md`](../docs/FEATURES.md), and the architectural contract is recorded in [`ADR-0089`](../docs/adr/0089-selectable-diagram-families.md).
